senses.gloss:
Ādipurāṇa
(‘the original म्य्थोलोग्य्’)
------------------------------------------
Every religion has three aspects: philosophy, म्य्थोलोग्य् and rituals. While philosophy tries to find solutions to the ultimate questions and problems of life, म्य्थोलोग्य् tries to explain the truths discovered by it, through stories, allegories and examples. The Hindu mythological lore, designated ‘purāṇa,’ does this and much more. It gives whole systems of knowledge in various fields whether allied to or even remotely connected with philo-sophy, or not. The Ādipurāṇa is one of the पुराणस् often included in the lists.
According to one tradition, it is the original purāṇa, as its very name implies, composed by ब्रह्मा the Creator himself.
Comprising four hundred thousand verses, it is the source book for all the other पुराणस् written by व्यास. The book however is not available now.
Among the extant पुराणस्, the Brahmapurāṇa is occasionally designated as Ādipurāṇa also. One Ādipurāṇa is sometimes listed among the minor पुराणस् known as उपपुराणस्. This book, now available in print is obviously a much later work. It is mainly the story of कृष्ण.
The Jaina tradition (digambara sect) also has an Ādipurāṇa, an incomplete work by one Jinasena, a part of which was added on later by another author Guṇabhadra. It describes the stories of Ṛṣabhadeva and भरत, the first two Tīrthaṅkaras.
See also PURĀṆAS and UPAPURĀṆAS.

Ādiśeṣa
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu mythological literature, आदिशेष is described as a mighty serpent of a thousand hoods on which he is supporting the world. He forms the bed on which Lord नारायण is reclining. अनन्त, Anantanāga, शेष and Śeṣanāga are his other names. Born as the son of Kadru and कश्यप he later on dropped out of the company of his brother-serpents since they illtreated his step-मोथेर् विनता who was a good and noble woman. He pleased ब्रह्मा, the Creator, by severe austerities and obtained the boon of the power to support the world on his hoods. Lord नारायण was pleased to make him his couch. लक्ष्मण and बलराम, the brothers of राम and कृष्ण, are said to be the incarnations of आदिशेष. So also पतञ्जलि, the promulgator of the योग system of philosophy.
It is obvious that this is a highly allegorical and symbolical picture. आदिशेष really stands for cosmic time and space which are ‘ananta,’ endless or infinite. Hence, the myth of आदिशेष supporting the world on his thousand hoods signifies that the created world comes into being in the infinite time and space and is sustained by them. The thousand hoods stand for the innumerable divisions of time and space.
The word ‘śeṣa’ means ‘what is left over’, ‘the remainder’. Since च्रेअतिओन् cannot proceed out of nothing, it is to be assumed that ‘something’ is left over (śeṣa) from the previous cycle of च्रेअतिओन्. So शेष represents the totality of jīvas or individual souls in their subtle forms left over from the previous cycle and needing more opportunities for redemption.
The serpent usually stands for काम or desire, which is always left over (śeṣa) even after acquiring and enjoying the desired object. Hence in a cosmic sense it can stand for the desire of the Lord to proceed with the next cycle of च्रेअतिओन् after rest.
Lord नारायण reclining upon the serpent couch can mean that desire for च्रेअतिओन् as also time and space form the basis, resting on which he proceeds with च्रेअतिओन्.
See also NĀRĀYAṆA.

Āditya-śānti-vrata
(‘religious vow to appease आदित्य or Sun-god’)
------------------------------------------
Vratas or religious vows and observances are a common form of practical religion in हिन्दुइस्म्. These vratas are undertaken either for fulfilling a desire with divine intervention or for expiating sin or even as observing a spiritual discipline.
The Ādityaśāntivrata can be observed on any Sunday associated with the Hastā-नक्षत्र. Worshipping the image of the Sun with 28 or 108 fuel sticks of the arka plant (Calatropis gigantea) is the main part of the ritual. These fuel sticks are to be offered with honey and ghee (or ghee and curds) in होम (fire sacrifice). The vrata can be repeated seven times.
See also VRATAS.

Ādiparva
------------------------------------------
Mahābhārata, the great epic of हिन्दुइस्म् and the biggest didactic work of poetry in world literature, is divided into eighteen books, each of which is known as a ‘parvan.’ Ādiparva forms the very first book. For details see under MAHĀBHĀRATA.

Ādimūrti
(‘the Original form’)
------------------------------------------
Viṣṇu, the central deity of the Hindu Trinity, manifests himself in several forms. ‘Ādimūrti’ is one of them. Considered as a minor manifestation, he is described in iconographical works as sitting upon the serpent आदिशेष, with the right leg hanging and the left as folded and resting upon the seat. Of the four hands, the two back hands hold as usual, the शङ्ख (conch) and चक्र (discus). The front right hand rests upon the seat whereas the front left is supported on the folded left knee. The colour of the figure is coral red and it is richly decorated with ornaments. The other two gods of the Trinity, ब्रह्मा and शिव, as also the sages भृगु and मार्कण्डेय are also shown, in a reveren-tial aspect.

Ādivāsīs
(‘Original inhabitants’)
------------------------------------------
The population of the आदिवासीस्, the original inhabitants of India or aboriginals—that is what the name signifies—exceeds thirty million. They are primarily to be found in north-east India, Bihar, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and parts of Maharashtra, Deccan and South India. How many of them are really the ‘original’ inhabitants and how many have come as migrants is anybody’s guess. The various tribes of आदिवासीस् largely inhabiting the mountain and jungle areas differ widely from one another with regard to racial characteristics, language, ड़ोओद् habits, modes of dress, means of occupation as also their cult and culture. By and large they are treated as belonging to हिन्दु चुल्तुरे.
Their religious beliefs and observances include the worship of nature and totems as also their ancestors and spirits. Taboos are many. Bloody sacrifices are common. Priests are sorcerers too and have a tight grip over the community. Modern एदुचतिओन्, wherever it has percolated, is fast changing the complexion of their life style.

Ādiśakti
(‘Primeval Power’)
------------------------------------------
The source and sustenance of all च्रेअतिओन् whether at the level of matter, मिन्द् or life, is one. It is called शक्ति (power or energy). हिन्दुइस्म् posits a cyclic theory of च्रेअतिओन् (sṛṣṭi), preservation (sthiti) and destruction (pralaya) and this goes on eternally. It is the शक्ति of God that is responsible for this. This शक्ति is usually conceived as a female deity, as the Consort of God. Since she is the original source, she is often called ‘Ādiśakti,’ the Primeval Power.
It is the Śaiva and शाक्त Āgama works that propound this theory of शक्ति, and She is fully identified with पार्वती, शिव’s Consort. Māyā (the illusory power of God) of Vedānta and दुर्गा of the पुराणस् are also called आदिशक्ति since they also are identified with पार्वती.
See also ŚAKTI.

āditya-darśana
(‘seeing the sun’)
------------------------------------------
Every Hindu has to undergo certain सṁस्कारस् or sacraments—religious rites conducive to inner evolution—at various stages of his life. The धर्मशास्त्रस् list them as sixteen; hence the name ‘ṣodaśa-सṁस्कारस्’ (ṣodaśa 16). One such ṣaṁskāra called ‘niṣkramaṇa’ (lit., ‘going out’) consists of taking the baby outside the lying-in chamber for the first time, to see the sun. This is ‘āditya-दर्शन.’ For details see NIṢKRAMAṆA.
See also SAṀSKĀRAS and ṢODAŚA-SAṀSKĀRAS.

Ādinātha
(‘the Primeval Lord’)
------------------------------------------
The esoteric नाथ चुल्त् which originated in Bengal and the followers of which are found in some parts of North India considers the Supreme Being as elusive and intangible, and as manifested in the universe created out of him. It designates him as ‘Ādinātha.’ Following in the footsteps of the Ṛgveda (10.129) and the opening verse of Manusaṁhitā, the नाथ चुल्त् describes the beginning of च्रेअतिओन् as starting from a bubble or an egg which appeared as a result of the impulse for च्रेअतिओन् in the infinite void and all-encompassing darkness. The egg hatched and out of it emerged ‘Ādinātha’ the primeval God. From his sweat was produced his spouse Ketakā or मनसा who in turn created ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and शिव. Further च्रेअतिओन् proceeded out of them.
The first of the nine Nātha gurus is also आदिनाथ.
See also NĀTHA-CULT.

Aditi
(‘the boundless’)
------------------------------------------
Aditi, the ‘devamātā’ (mother of the gods) is one of the few goddesses mentioned in the Ṛgveda and other Vedic literature. She is often associated with दिति, her sister, and मोथेर् of the दैत्यस् (demons). She is eulogised as the boundless and identified with practically everything in the created world. She is the sky and the air. The three aspects of time are also she. She has become all the human beings, nay, even the gods. She is the मोथेर् and she is the ड़थेर् too. That is why supplications are made to her to confer her blessings on children and cattle as also for the removal of sins (vide ऋग्वेद Saṁhitā 1.89.10).
In the mythological lore of the वेदस् she is usually described as one of the daughters of दक्ष, though sometimes she is said to be his मोथेर्. There are also passages which mention her as the wife of विष्णु instead of कश्यप. However according to most of the accounts she was married to the sage कश्यप for whom she bore several sons. The gods being her sons are called Āditeyas. Sometimes the eight Ādityas are described as her sons. Out of these eight, she is said to have cast out the last son Mārttaṇḍa.
Coming to the उपनिषद्स्, the word ‘Aditi’ is used to denote death, the devourer (ad to devour) (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5), and the deity presiding over the earth (Mahānārayaṇa Upaniṣad 28.1) as also the jīvātman or the individual सोउल् (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.7).
In the epics and the पुराणस् she is always depicted as the daughter of दक्ष, wife of कश्यप and मोथेर् of gods including the वामन इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु. इन्द्र is said to have picked up a pair of divine kuṇḍalas (ear-rings) as they were thrown up by the churning of the primeval ocean (See SAMUDRAMATHANA) and presented them to अदिति. But the demon नरकासुर Bhauma (the son of Bhūmi or earth) stole them from her. It was कृष्ण who recovered and restored them to her.
Aditi is also the name of a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे on the bank of the river गङ्गा.

Āditya-hṛdaya
(‘the heart or the essence of आदित्य’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu hymnal literature is as vast as it is deep. Quite a few of these hymns, whether they contain praises of the Lord or expound some philosophical doctrines, are often used for ceremonial chanting, considering them as mantras (esoteric words and sentences) capable of fulfilling one’s desires. The Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, though a voluminuous work, strangely enough, contains only one such hymn; strangely enough because, the Mahā-bhārata, the other epic, as also the पुराणस् contain scores of them. This hymn known as the ‘Ādityahṛdaya’ occurs in the Yuddhakāṇḍa (sarga 105).
After the first round of battle with रावण, राम was rather tired and anxious as to how he could vanquish his formidable enemy. Just at that time, अगस्त्य the sage of the विन्ध्य fame, who was among those that had gathered to witness the battle, came forward to reveal a secret with the help of which राम could conquer रावण and fulfil the mission of his life. The secret was the Ādityahṛdaya hymn by reciting which he could get enough power to destroy his foe. Being initiated into its mysteries by अगस्त्य, राम recited it thrice, became imbued with energy and enthusiasm and achieved victory with ease.
Whether the Ādityahṛdaya comprises the entire chapter or part of it only (e.g., verses 6 to 21) is a point on which there are differences of opinion. Verses 1 to 5 form the introduction and eulogise the hymn. Verses 6 to 21 describe आदित्य or the Sun-god, his various names and attributes. Verses 22 to 25 describe his power and give the phalaśruti (the benefits of recitation). Verse 26 gives the viniyoga (the method and purpose of recitation). Verses 27 to 31 complete the narration of the story.
Here are a few of the epithets which the hymn uses to describe and eulogise आदित्य: He is so effulgent that even the gods adore him. In fact he is the very personification of all gods including the Trinity. It is he that is manifested as the leaders of the eight quarters. He is the creator and sustainer of the world. It is again he that destroys the world at the end of the cycle of च्रेअतिओन्. He is manifested in everything that is created.
The proper recitation of the hymn will free a man from all troubles and tribulations and fulfil the wishes of his heart.
Every मन्त्र has a ṛṣi (the seer to whom it was revealed), a छन्दस् (the poetical metre) and a devatā (the deity to whom it is addressed), who are to be adored at the beginning of a ceremonial recitation. In the case of this hymn (which is considered as a मन्त्र), अगस्त्य is the ṛṣi and anuṣṭubh is the छन्दस्. As regards the devatā, some state that ब्रह्मा residing in the sun is the deity whereas others consider राम the Supreme God, the internal ruler of the sun, is himself the deity. The viniyoga or purpose is to obtain supreme knowledge or victory in all walks of life.
Any Sunday on which there is a सङ्क्रान्ति (movement of the sun from one zodiacal sign to the next) is believed to be very holy and suitable for the recitation of this hymn. Repeating it 108 times in a Sun-temple and observing a fast in the night are considered to be highly meritorious.

Āditya
(‘son/sons of अदिति’)
------------------------------------------
Āditya is one of the well-known epithets of the sun.
The Ādityas, the sons of अदिति, repre-sent a group of deities. They are six in the Ṛgveda, eight in most of the ब्राह्मणस् (except the Śatapatha) and twelve in the later mythological lore. They can be described as the personifications of the laws that rule the universe and the human society. They regulate the relationships of human beings among themselves and with the forces of nature.
Since आदित्य is one of the names of the sun, the Ādityas can be considered as imperishable beings, the gods of light, by whom all kinds of luminous life are manifested and sustained in this universe.
The twelve Ādityas are: मित्र (the friend), वरुण (one who encompasses and binds), अर्यमन् (the destroyer of foes), दक्ष (the skilful), भग (the giver), Aṁśa (the liberal), Tvaṣṭṛ (the shaper), Savitṛ (the vivifier), पूषन् (the nourisher), Śakra (the mighty), Vivasvat (the resplendent) and विष्णु (the pervader).
Sometimes, these twelve are linked with the twelve aspects of the sun spread over the twelve months and hence des-cribed as the twelve spokes of the wheel of time.
See also SŪRYA.

Ādityatīrtha
(‘place of पिल्ग्रिमगे connec-ted with आदित्य or Sun-god’)
------------------------------------------
Places of पिल्ग्रिमगे have always played a very important part in the life of a devout Hindu. Endowed with natural beauty and conducive to peace and blessed-ness these places have been attracting millions of pious pilgrims since millennia.
Ādityatīrtha is one of the less known places of पिल्ग्रिमगे mentioned in some of the Hindu scriptures (vide Śalyaparva, ch. 49 of Mahābhārata). Situated on the bank of the now invisible सरस्वती रिवेर्, the place got its name on account of its association with आदित्य (Sun) who performed a sacrifice there and obtained lordship over all bright objects. It was here that Lord विष्णु killed the demons मधु and कैटभ.
Again it was in this sacred place that great sages like व्यास, कृष्ण and शुक performed austerities and gained perfection.
The Padmapurāṇa locates it at the confluence of the river Sābhramatī with the sea.
See also TĪRTHAS.

Ādityavrata
(‘vrata to please आदित्य’)
------------------------------------------
A ब्रह्मचारिन् (celibate student) living in the होउसे of the आचार्य (preceptor) had to observe several vratas (religious observances) as part of the student-life. Whenever the study of new sections of the वेदस् had to be commenced he had to prepare himself physically and mentally for the same. For instance the followers of Sāmaveda were required to perform five vratas before studying its several sections: godānika, vrātika, आदित्य, aupaniṣada and jyeṣṭhasāma vratas.
Ādityavrata was considered as optional by some authorities, whereas the other vratas were compulsory. It had to be performed before beginning the study of the शुक्रिय section (last part of the Āraṇyaka) of the सामवेद.
Before beginning the vrata nāndī-mukha-śrāddha (See ĀBHYUDAYIKA ŚRĀDDHA.) had to be performed and उपनयन saṁskāra had to be undergone once again, followed by ājyahoma (offering ghee into the fire) with आदित्य mantras. During the period of the vrata which lasted for a year, the ब्रह्मचारिन् had to wear only one cloth and avoid taking protection against the sun’s rays by contrivances like umbrella. Of course, taking shelter in the होउसे or under trees was allowed. Also, he was prohibited from entering into more than knee-deep water, for bath. The vrata had to be concluded with offering चरु (porridge of unpounded rice) to इन्द्र, repeating the ājyahoma and gifting a cow to the आचार्य (preceptor).

Ādityapurāṇa
(‘purāṇa concerning आदित्य or Sun-god’)
------------------------------------------
Purāṇas or the mythological lore of the Hindus are a vast body of literature dealing with not only philosophical and religious subjects but also cultural and even mundane subjects. They are divided into two broad groups: The Mahāpurāṇas (the great, big or main पुराणस्) and the उपपुराणस् (small or subsidiary पुराणस्). Ādityapurāṇa, a purāṇa dealing with the deity आदित्य (Sun-god), is often mentioned in the latter group. The book itself is not available now, except for some quotations incorporated by the dharmaśāstra literature. These quotations concern the following subjects: राजधर्म (duties of the king), दान (gifts), śrāddha (obsequial offerings), vrata (religious vows and obser-vances) and शौच (ceremonial purity).
The Matsyapurāṇa (53.62) as also Al Beruni (A. D. 1030) mention this purāṇa.
See also PURĀṆAS.
